narrative.text: Cover page for The MAPS Toolkit: mHealth Assessment and Planning for Scale, published with the Global mHealth Initiative at Johns Hopkins University, WHO, HRP, and the United Nations Foundation.

Provides WHO Library Cataloguing-in-Publication data (ISBN 978 92 4 150951 0, NLM classification WA 310), 2015 copyright and licensing notices, legal disclaimers, cover photo credit (D-tree International eNutrition application in Zanzibar), and suggested citation for The MAPS Toolkit.

Presents the table of contents for The MAPS Toolkit, covering the front matter, introduction, project overview sheet, the six axes of scale (Groundwork, Partnerships, Financial health, Technology & architecture, Operations, and Monitoring & evaluation—each with a thematic overview, self-assessment questions, and planning and guidance), the summary scorecard, references, and two annexes.

Foreword by Flavia Bustreo (WHO) and Kate Dodson (United Nations Foundation) tracing the origins of the MAPS Toolkit to the Every Woman Every Child (EWEC) Innovation Working Group (IWG) Catalytic mHealth Grant Mechanism established by Norway in 2011 across 15 countries, and positioning the Toolkit for the transition from the Millennium Development Goals to the Sustainable Development Goals.

Acknowledges the authors (Jessica Rothstein and Tigest Tamrat under the guidance of Garrett Mehl at WHO and Alain Labrique at JHU-GmI), technical contributors, field experts, country-level partner organizations, testing and validation reviewers, the 26 IWG Catalytic mHealth Grant Mechanism projects, and Norad/WHO leadership.

Executive summary introducing the MAPS Toolkit as an iterative self-assessment and planning guide for project managers and teams already deploying an mHealth product, structured around six axes of scale: Groundwork, Partnerships, Financial health, Technology & architecture, Operations, and Monitoring & evaluation.

Lists acronyms and abbreviations used throughout the MAPS Toolkit, spanning digital health standards and systems (API, DHIS, eLMIS, HL7, HMIS, HRIS, ICD, OCL, OpenHIE, OpenSRP, SNOMED CT), organizations and networks (AeHIN, ANDH, CHAI, GSMA, HRP, ITU, IWG, JHU-GmI, KEMRI, MAMA, Norad, PMNCH, UNF, WHO), and mHealth programmes (m4RH, mNDCC, MOTECH, TextIT).

First half of the Key terminology glossary (Architecture through Mobile money), defining core mHealth and scale-up concepts including champions, client beneficiaries, core partners, data dashboard, data dictionary, data privacy, data quality assurance, data standards, eHealth, enabling environment, end-users, endgame, evaluation and formative research, health system constraints, interoperability, latency, mHealth strategy, and mobile aggregator.

Second half of the Key terminology glossary (Mobile network operator through Value proposition), defining MNOs, payers (distinguished from funders), pilot testing, process monitoring, mHealth product, programme fidelity, scaling up, secondary users, SMS, software, standard operating procedures (SOPs), stress tests, sustainability, total cost of ownership (TCO), value chain analysis, and value proposition.
Section divider page introducing the Introduction chapter of the MAPS Toolkit.

Provides background on scaling up mHealth in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), contrasting small-scale pilots and broad ecosystem-level literature with the MAPS Toolkit's actionable, project-level approach to continuous scale-up and sustainability, alongside sidebar definitions of scaling up, sustainability, and the three endgame models (government adoption, commercial adoption, and hybrid).

Explains the dual purpose of the MAPS Toolkit—Assess (via scored self-assessment questions) and Plan (via targeted guidance)—and introduces the cyclical Assess–Plan–Improve conceptual model (Figure 1) and the six axes of scale (Figure 2) with concise one-sentence descriptions of each axis.

Presents Figure 3 mapping the six axes of scale to their constituent domains (Parameters of scale, Contextual environment, Scientific basis; Strategic engagement, Partnership sustainability; Financial management, Financial model; Data, Interoperability, Adaptability; Personnel, Training & support, Outreach & sensitization, Contingency planning; Process monitoring, Evaluation research) and summarizes how MAPS was developed under the Norad-funded UNF–WHO IWG Catalytic mHealth Grant Mechanism.

Describes the three-part chapter structure for each axis (A. Thematic overview, B. Self-assessment, and C. Planning and guidance with Tips and considerations, Lessons from the field, and Resources) and specifies the target audience and eligibility criteria for projects using MAPS (deployed mHealth product past proof-of-concept with a defined mHealth strategy and scale-up endgame).

Explains how to conduct the MAPS self-assessment (either via individual specialist completion followed by a team review or via sequential team meetings over 1.5–2 hours), when to use the Toolkit as a baseline and periodic tracking tool, and how to respond to self-assessment questions using No/Yes or the four-stage progression (No, In progress, Performed, Documented) plus Not applicable (N/A).

Provides Table 1 defining and illustrating the four response options (No = 0, In progress = 1, Performed = 2, Documented = 3) using electricity constraints from SAQ 14-1 (solar chargers for health workers), and explains the three-level scoring system (overall, axis, and domain scores) using axis scorecards and the final scorecard.

Explains how project teams should use SAQ results to identify weak domains, consult planning resources, and periodically course-correct, accompanied by Figure 4 illustrating a worked sample SAQ (14-1 on addressing connectivity and electricity constraints, earning 4 out of 9 points).

Presents the baseline Project overview sheet worksheet capturing Project Details (date, project and organization names, mHealth strategy, technologies and communication channels), Current Project Status (coverage, start date and duration, operating geographies), and Vision for Scale (scale-up goals and anticipated time frame).
Chapter divider page for Axis 1: Groundwork, highlighting its position among the six axes of scale.

Introduces the Axis 1 (Groundwork) thematic overview across its three domains (Domain 1: Parameters of scale, Domain 2: Contextual environment, Domain 3: Scientific basis) and details Domain 1, guiding teams to articulate target health outcomes, health system constraints, scale-up metrics, quantifiable targets, and eligible population denominators.

Presents Table 2 on metrics for measuring scale-up success—Growth (client, e.g. FHI 360 m4RH in Tanzania), Adoption (institutional, e.g. KEMRI TextIT in Kenya), and Expansion (geo-political, e.g. JSI cStock across all 29 districts in Malawi)—Defines government adoption, commercial adoption (e.g. Changamka Linda Jamii with Safaricom), and hybrid endgames, and introduces Domain 2 (Contextual environment) covering policy and technical environments.

Completes Domain 2 with mHealth landscape assessment and details Domain 3 (Scientific basis), explaining how to align with validated health interventions, evaluate the four stages of mHealth evidence (Functionality, Usability, Efficacy, and Effectiveness), validate strategy components, and conduct local formative research and cultural contextualization.

Presents the Axis 1 Self-Assessment Questions for Domain 1 (Parameters of scale, 8 points total), specifically SAQ 1-1 (6 points) on articulating RMNCH life-stage health outcomes and interventions, targeted health system constraints (availability, cost, efficiency, quality, utilization, information, acceptability), and operationalized scale-up metrics (growth, adoption, geo-political expansion).

Continues Axis 1 self-assessment with SAQ 1-2 (2 points) on specifying the endgame strategy (government adoption, commercial adoption, or hybrid) and Domain 2 (Contextual environment, 22 points total), covering SAQ 2-1 (6 points) on national health/eHealth policy alignment and working group participation and SAQ 2-2 (8 points) on network coverage and electricity reach and reliability.

Presents SAQ 2-3 (8 points) on assessing the local mHealth landscape and Domain 3 (Scientific basis, 30 points total), including SAQ 3-1a (8 points) on evidence across functionality, usability, efficacy, and effectiveness and SAQ 3-1b (4 points) on validating content and operational procedures against evidence-based guidelines or pilot studies.

Presents SAQ 3-2 (18 points, scored 0–3 across No, In progress, Performed, and Documented) assessing local appropriateness across six items: formative research, pilot study in a comparable setting, local health system constraints, local health service capacity, integration with health worker workflows, and sociocultural/gender norms.

Provides the Axis 1 (Groundwork) scorecard for tallying points and calculating domain percentages across Domain 1: Parameters of scale (8 points), Domain 2: Contextual environment (22 points), and Domain 3: Scientific basis (30 points), and averaging the three domain percentages to obtain the overall Axis 1 score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 1 and provides Domain 1 tips and frameworks for articulating how mHealth strategies address health system constraints and advance universal health coverage, citing Labrique et al. (2013) on 12 common applications and Mehl & Labrique (2014) on prioritizing integrated mHealth strategies.

Provides Domain 2 (Contextual environment) planning guidance on joining communities of practice and technical working groups to share knowledge and map the digital health environment, profiling the mHealth Working Group, Asia eHealth Information Network (AeHIN), African Network for Digital Health (ANDH), HealthEnabled Africa, and the ICT4CHW Google Group.

Provides Domain 3 (Scientific basis) guidance on leveraging the existing evidence base for health interventions, shares a field lesson from KEMRI's TextIT PMTCT SMS programme in Kenya on using focus group formative research to personalize messages and include male partners, and introduces JSI's Pathway to Supply Chain Sustainability planning tool for government adoption.

Summarizes four foundational planning and contextual-assessment resources for Axis 1: K4Health's mHealth Planning Guide (2014), HealthEnabled's How to Approach mHealth (Keisling, 2015), the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit (2012), and PMNCH's ICT for Women's and Children's Health: A Planning Workbook (2014).

Describes country-level feasibility and landscape-mapping resources for Axis 1: GSMA Country Feasibility Reports (2014) across 10 African countries, HealthEnabled African Digital Dashboards (2015), USAID/African Strategies for Health's mHealth Database, the Center for Health Market Innovations (CHMI) Health Program Database, and the mHealth Working Group Inventory.

Concludes the Axis 1 resource list with four global mHealth project repositories and compendia: the GSMA mHealth Tracker, the WHO–ITU Global eHealth Projects Repository, mRegistry.org (WHO HRP, JHU-GmI, UNICEF, mPowering Frontline Health Workers), and the USAID/ASH mHealth Compendium series.
Chapter divider page for Axis 2: Partnerships.

Introduces the Axis 2 (Partnerships) thematic overview across Domain 4 (Strategic engagement) and Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability), detailing how project teams assess internal competencies to identify core and supporting external partners and tailor value propositions to foster stakeholder buy-in.

Presents Table 3 mapping notions of value across seven potential partner types (MOH/government, MNO, field-level NGO/CBO, end-users, donors, academia, and insurers) and outlines Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability), emphasizing cultivating organizational champions and establishing formal governance structures (steering committees, MoUs, and vendor contracts).

Presents the Axis 2 Self-Assessment Questions for Domain 4 (Strategic engagement, 48 points total), covering SAQ 4-1a (9 points) on defining internal competencies, required external partner types, and timing, and SAQ 4-1b (27 points) on partnership maturity across nine partner/vendor categories (MOH, financing, MNO/aggregator, NGO/CBO, technology, hardware/service, marketing, evaluation/research, and health content).

Continues Axis 2 self-assessment with SAQ 4-2 (12 points) on communicating the product's value proposition and alignment with partner, local government, and global health priorities, and introduces Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability, 50 points total) with SAQ 5-1a (9 points) on fostering champions and SAQ 5-1b (10 points) on evaluating the first champion's authority, stability, resources, scope awareness, and demonstrated commitment.

Concludes the Axis 2 Self-Assessment Questions with SAQ 5-1c (10 points) assessing a second champion's advocacy capacity, SAQ 5-2a (12 points) on inclusive governance mechanisms (representative steering committee, regular meetings, terms of reference, and partner feedback), and SAQ 5-2b (9 points) on shared agreement with core partners regarding project vision, scale-up scope/goals, and joint workplan/timeline.

Provides the Axis 2 (Partnerships) scorecard for calculating scores across Domain 4: Strategic engagement (48 points, with denominator adjustments for N/A items in SAQ 4-1b) and Domain 5: Partnership sustainability (50 points, or 30 points if champion questions 5-1b/5-1c are N/A), averaging the two domain percentages for the Axis 2 score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 2 and Domain 4 (Strategic engagement), advising teams to map partners by both technical competencies and strategic assets (visibility, networks, gatekeepers) and sharing a field lesson on continuous engagement from MAMA South Africa's transition into the national Department of Health's MomConnect initiative.

Provides Domain 4 guidance on starting partner negotiations early to accommodate turnover and legal/MoU delays, articulating partner 'gives and gets' value propositions (illustrated by India's SERP mNDCC nutrition monitoring tool adopted by the Andhra Pradesh government and expanded to 6000 villages with the World Bank), and evaluating inter-departmental political dynamics and mandates.

Provides Domain 5 (Partnership sustainability) guidance on diversifying partners to avoid single-vendor lock-in, cultivating backup or team champions to mitigate political turnover, and positioning government at the forefront of coordination—illustrated by CHAI Malawi's MOH-convened RapidSMS steering committee and Rwanda's MOH eHealth Technical Working Group (TWG).

Advises teams to document partnership terms of engagement (roles, intellectual property/licensing, human and financial resource commitments, branding, and vendor billing structures) in MoUs and contracts, and summarizes two partnership resources: PMNCH's ICT for Women's and Children's Health Planning Workbook (2014) and the WHO & UNF Practical Guide for Engaging with Mobile Network Operators in mHealth for RMNCH (2015).

Concludes the Axis 2 resource list with four publications on MNO partnerships and governance: GSMA mWomen's Mutual Value, Mutual Gain (2014), Advanced Development for Africa's Scaling Up Mobile Health: Developing mHealth Partnerships for Scale (2013), Miller's Fifty Tips for Your Statement of Work (2007), and UNF's ICT4SOML Nigeria Situation Analysis (2013).
Chapter divider page for Axis 3: Financial health.

Introduces the Axis 3 (Financial health) thematic overview across Domain 6 (Financial management) and Domain 7 (Financial model), detailing programme costs (recurring fixed, variable, and one-time capital costs, in-kind contributions, cost-sharing, and regular budget revision) and end-user technology and non-technology costs.

Completes Domain 6 with health system costs (provider workload and supply ripple effects from increased care demand) and 5-year cost forecasting using total cost of ownership (TCO) and cost drivers, and details Domain 7 (Financial model), covering stakeholder value chain analysis, dynamic business planning, and diversifying funders and payers.

Presents the Axis 3 Self-Assessment Questions for Domain 6 (Financial management, 45 points total), covering SAQ 6-1 (18 points) on programme-level expenditure tracking, phase-based costing, capital/recurring/variable categorization, in-kind valuation, cost-sharing, and budget revision protocols; SAQ 6-2 (6 points) on end-user technology and non-technology costs; and SAQ 6-3 (9 points) on health system demand, provider time, and commodity costs.

Continues Axis 3 self-assessment with SAQ 6-4 (12 points) on forecasting 5-year total cost of ownership, cost drivers, economies of scale, and costing assumptions/risks, and introduces Domain 7 (Financial model, 36 points total) with SAQ 7-1 (12 points) on value chain analysis and quantifying tangible/intangible status quo costs and SAQ 7-2 (12 points) on developing a shareable business, resource mobilization, and marketing plan.

Concludes the Axis 3 Self-Assessment Questions with SAQ 7-3 (12 points) on sustainable funding choices: exploring diverse funding streams (including non-health sectors), identifying main and alternative payers across the value chain, planning payer engagement, and mitigating payer-transition risks.

Provides the Axis 3 (Financial health) scorecard for tallying points and calculating domain percentages across Domain 6: Financial management (45 points) and Domain 7: Financial model (36 points), averaging the two percentages to compute the overall Axis 3 score.

Introduces Section C (Planning and guidance) for Axis 3 and Domain 6 (Financial management), highlighting commonly overlooked scale-up costs when forecasting: transition and capacity-building costs when transferring ownership to a Ministry of Health, technology adaptation and API integration costs, and legal/travel costs for advocacy and partner contract negotiation.
